translations.text: The story of Thecla, the disciple of Paul the apostle.
The story of Thecla, the disciple of Paul the apostle.
When Paul was going up to the city of Iconium after his persecution, Demas and Hermogenes accompanied him, bronze workers and smiths who were full of turmoil.
They made grand speeches and spoke with Paul as though he were their dear friend. Paul, however, was looking toward the dwelling place of Christ’s grace.
He did nothing offensive toward them, but loved them sincerely. He loved them so much that all the words
of the Lord, of his teaching and its interpretation, and of the birth and resurrection of the Beloved, he settled in their souls through the mighty deeds of Christ.
He showed them how he had been revealed to him, and told them about it in words. Now there was a man named Onesiphorus.
He heard that Paul had come to the city of Iconium, and went out with the sons of Simon and with Zeno
and with his wife to meet Paul and welcome him. For Titus had told him what Paul looked like.
For Onesiphorus did not know him in person, but only in spirit. And [?] he took his stand at the crossroads, on the highway that led
to Lystra. He stood waiting for him, examining those who passed back and forth according to the identifying details Titus had given him.
He saw Paul coming. He was a man of medium height, with thin hair, and his legs were slightly bowed.
His heels were unsteady. He had large eyes, his eyebrows met, and his nose was somewhat long.
He was full of kindness and compassion. Sometimes he looked like a human being, and sometimes he looked like an angel.
When Paul saw Onesiphorus, he rejoiced. Onesiphorus said to him, “Peace to you, apostle of the Blessed One.” Paul said to him, “Peace to you,
Onesiphorus, and to everyone in your household.” But Demas and Hermogenes were filled with envy, and their jealousy grew. They said to Paul,
“Do we not belong to the Blessed One? You have never greeted us like that.” He answered them, “Because I do not see deeds of righteousness in you.”
Onesiphorus said to them, “If you are anything, come to my house as well and rest.”
When Paul entered Onesiphorus’s house, there was great joy there. They wept on their knees and prayed,
and broke bread. Paul came forward and spoke God’s words to him concerning self-control and the resurrection of the dead. He said,
“Blessed are those who are pure in heart, for they will see God. Blessed are those who have kept
their bodies holy, for they will be called temples of God. Blessed are those who exercise self-control,
for God will speak with them. Blessed are those who have rejected this world, for they will please God.
Blessed are those who have wives as though they had none, for they will inherit the earth. Blessed are those who have the fear of God in their hearts,
for they will be called angels. Blessed are those who tremble at the words of God that they hear, for God will call them.”
Blessed are those who have received the wisdom of Jesus Christ, for they will be called children of God.
Blessed are those who have kept their baptism, for they will rest with the Father in heaven and with his beloved Son.
Blessed are those who have received Christ’s assurance, for they will be in great light. Blessed are those
who have departed from this body for the love of God, for they will inherit eternal life and stand at the right hand of the Son of God.
Blessed are the merciful, for they will receive mercy from God, and on the day of judgment they will receive the kingdom.
Blessed are the bodies and spirits of virgins, for they will please God, and the reward of their chastity will not be lost.
For through the Father’s word, deeds leading to life will be found for them on the day of his Son, and they will have rest forever.
While Paul was speaking of these mighty things of God among the congregation in the house of Onesiphorus,
a virgin named Thecla, the daughter of Theocleia, who was betrothed to Thamyris, came and sat at a window near their roofs.
She listened to Paul’s words as he spoke about chastity, and she did not leave that window.
Night and day she listened to Paul’s prayer and marveled at the faith. She also saw many women
going in to Paul to hear his words as he taught the commandments of God.
She too longed to hear Paul’s words, for she had not seen what he looked like; she had only heard his words.
She would not leave that window at all. Then her mother sent for Thamyris, her fiancé. When Thamyris, her fiancé, heard that his mother-in-law had called him,
he ran and came to her, as though she were now giving Thecla to him to take in marriage. Thamyris spoke and said
to his mother-in-law, “Where is Thecla, my fiancée, so that I may see her?”
Theocleia answered him, “I have something strange to tell you, Thamyris. For three days and three nights now, Thecla, your fiancée,
has not risen from that window, not even to eat or drink. Instead, her eyes are fixed on a stranger, and she gazes at him.
He speaks empty and foolish words as though they were delightful. I am so astonished
at how quickly sensible virgins are led captive after him, to their great harm. I tell you, Thamyris,
he has corrupted the whole city of Iconium, and your fiancée Thecla as well. Many women and young men go in to him,
and he teaches them to worship one God and live chastely. Thecla, too, has become bound to him like a spider to its web. She has been seized by a new desire
and an evil passion. Her eyes are fixed on whatever comes from that room, and she will not leave that window,
not even to eat or drink. The girl has been swallowed up by it. But you, Thamyris, go to her and speak with her,
for she is betrothed to you.” Thamyris, her fiancé, approached her, both because he loved her and because he stood in awe of her modesty.
He answered her, “Thecla, you are betrothed to me. Why have you acted this way? What is this evil frenzy that has taken hold of you?”
“Turn toward Thamyris, your betrothed, and show him some respect.” Her mother also spoke to her and said, “Why are you looking down like this,”
“and giving no answer? Instead, you are acting like a madwoman.” When the members of their household saw her, they wept.

Thamyris wept because his betrothed was being separated from him; her mother, because she was being separated from her daughter; and the servant women, because they were being separated from their mistress.
There was great sorrow and distress in their house. Yet Thecla paid no attention to any of this. Instead, her mind was intent on hearing Paul’s words.
Then Thamyris, her betrothed, went downstairs and rushed out into the marketplace. He watched those who went in and out to see Paul.
Suddenly he saw two men quarreling bitterly with one another. Thamyris approached them and said to them,
“Tell me who you are. And who is this man inside with you, who leads the souls of young women and virgins astray and commands that there should be no marriages,”
“but that they should live this way? I am willing to give you a great deal of money if you will tell me about him, for I am a leading man of this city.”
When Demas and Hermogenes saw him, they came over to him and answered, “As for this man you have spoken about, we do not know who he is.”
“But he separates young men from virgins and virgins from young men, and tells them, ‘You cannot rise from the dead”
“unless you keep yourselves chaste.’” Thamyris answered them, “Come with me to my house, my friends, and rest at my home.”
They went with him to a great dinner, abundant food, lavish luxury, and splendid tables.
Thamyris entertained them because he loved Thecla, his betrothed, and wanted to take her as his wife among women, on the day when his anger flared up.
While they were reclining at the meal, Thamyris spoke to them: “Tell me, my friends, what teachings he teaches, so that I too may know.”
“For there are quite a few people who complain about him. I too am distressed about my betrothed, because she has fallen in love with a stranger, and I am being separated”
“from her.” Demas and Hermogenes answered him with one voice, “Thamyris, bring him before Castelius the governor and say,”
“‘This man teaches a new doctrine, and he is a Christian.’ Then he will immediately put him to death, and you will marry Thecla, your betrothed.”
“And we will teach you about the resurrection of the dead that he teaches.” When Thamyris heard these words, he was filled with envy and jealousy. He rose early in the morning
and went to the house of Onesiphorus with the city’s leaders and many men carrying clubs. He spoke out and said, “Paul, you have ruined the city of Iconium,”
“and my betrothed, so that she will not marry me. Come to Castelius the governor!” The whole city said, “[?] Away with him! He is a sorcerer, for he is corrupting all our wives.”
The whole crowd was persuaded. Paul was taken away under arrest and stood before the governor. Thamyris spoke out and said to the governor in a loud voice,
“We do not know who this man is, and he does not allow virgins to marry men. Let him tell you why he teaches this doctrine.”
Demas and Hermogenes, the metalworkers, who were full of troublemaking, approached Thamyris and said to him, “Say that he is a Christian, and then”
“he will put him to death immediately.” When the governor heard the words of Thamyris and of that whole crowd who were holding Paul under arrest,
They saw the governor summon Paul and say to him, “Tell me, Paul, who are you, and what do you teach?
For there are many who accuse you.” Then Paul raised his voice and said, “Today I will explain what I teach.
Listen, governor: I teach about the living God, the God who does not repay anyone with harm, the God who needs nothing.
But human lives matter to him, and he sent me to rescue them from destruction and impurity,
and from all deadly desires, so that they may sin no more. This is why God sent me, the one whom I proclaim
and whose good news I announce, so that all people may place their hope in him. For he took care of them and rescued the nations from error [?], so that they might sin no more
and no longer live in confusion, but have reverence within them through faith in God, and truly know reverence and love.
And if I teach what [?] has revealed to me, what am I guilty of, governor?” When the governor heard these words, he ordered
that Paul be bound and taken to prison until he had an opportunity to hear him properly. That same night, Thecla
took her bracelets and gave them to the doorkeeper of their house. He opened the door for her, and she went out and went to the chief jailer, who was guarding Paul.
She gave him her gold mirror so that he would take her in to Paul, and he brought her in. She came and sat at Paul’s feet,
listening to the great deeds of God. Paul was not troubled, but openly taught God’s commandments
to everyone who was with him. And Thecla, with great joy, kept kissing the bonds and chains
that were on Paul’s hands and feet. When Thecla’s family and her fiancé looked for her, saying that she had vanished completely,
they went around searching for her in the streets. A fellow servant of the doorkeeper came and informed on him,
saying, “I saw Thecla during the night giving her bracelets to the doorkeeper. He opened the door for her, and she went out.”
When they flogged that doorkeeper, he confessed and told them, “She went out and said to me,
‘Look, I am going to that stranger, where he is imprisoned.’” They went as the doorkeeper had told them,
and found her sitting at Paul’s feet, together with many other people. They were listening to the great deeds of the Most High.
Thamyris and many other people left there in great anger and went and told the governor what had happened.
Then the governor said, “Bring Paul.” The young men ran and unbound Paul, and they dragged him from the prison
into the governor’s presence. Thecla rolled about and wept at the place where Paul had been sitting
while imprisoned and teaching God’s commandments. Then suddenly the governor gave another order, saying, “Bring Thecla, the woman betrothed to Thamyris.”
Thamyris and many other people ran and seized Thecla, and they dragged her to the governor.
When the governor saw her, he was deeply distressed on her account. But Thecla stood before him with great joy and was not troubled.
Then suddenly all the people shouted, saying, “Destroy this magician!” But he said nothing against Paul.
Then the governor sat on the judgment seat. He and his companions stood up, summoned Thecla, and said to her, “Why have you not married your fiancé
according to the law of the people of Iconium?” But Thecla stood looking at Paul and gave the governor no answer.
Then her mother shouted, saying, “Burn this senseless woman in the middle of the theater, so that all the women who see her [?] who follow this teaching may be afraid.”
When the governor heard this, he was deeply distressed for her. Then he gave orders, and they flogged Paul and took him outside the city.
He sentenced Thecla to be burned in the middle of the theater. The governor got up and went to the theater, together with all the people, to see Thecla burning in the fire.
Just as a ewe in the mountains searches for her shepherd, so Thecla searched to see where Paul was.
As she looked over that whole crowd, she saw the Lord Jesus Christ sitting near her in the likeness of Paul.
Thecla spoke and said, “So Paul has come and sat opposite me, as though I could not endure what has come upon me.”
She kept looking toward him, with her eyes fixed on him. Then the Lord rose from there and ascended into heaven. And they brought
wood—the boys and the young women—and placed it in the theater to burn Thecla. They brought her naked into the theater.
When the governor saw her, he wept and marveled at the strength she had. They piled up the wood.
The young men took hold of her to help her climb onto the fire. As soon as Thecla climbed up, she stretched out her hands in the shape of a cross and went up onto the fire.
When the flames rose, not even a single part of her hair was singed, because God had compassion on her.
The sound of her cry rose from the earth, and a rain cloud spread overhead. Hailstones [?] and water poured down in abundance.
Many of those people who were sitting and watching perished. The fire went out, and Thecla survived. Meanwhile, Paul was fasting,
together with Onesiphorus, his wife, and his children, in a tomb that stood open beside the road to Iconium.
After they had been fasting for many days, the children said to Paul, “We are hungry.”
They had nothing with which to buy bread, for Onesiphorus had left his house and his possessions,
and he and his household had gone out with Paul. Then Paul took off his tunic, gave it to the boy, and said to him, “Go and sell it, my son.
Buy plenty of bread and come back.” The boy went to buy bread and saw Thecla, their neighbor, and was astonished.
He said to her, “Thecla, where are you going?” She said to him, “I am looking for Paul, now that I have escaped the fire.”
The boy said to her, “Come with me, and I will take you to him. He is pleading and weeping, and he has been fasting for six days now,
praying to God for you.” Thecla came with him to that tomb. She entered and stood over Paul.
She found him kneeling and praying, saying, “Our Father in heaven, I ask you,
“Do not let the fire come near Thecla, but put it out around her, because she is yours.” Now Thecla, who was standing behind him,
opened her mouth and said, “Father who made heaven and earth, you are the Father of the Holy One. I thank you because you made me
and kept me alive so that I might see Paul.” Paul stood up and saw her. Then Paul spoke and said, “God,
who searches hearts, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, I thank you because you brought out of the fire what I asked you for.
You have allowed me and these people with me to see her. And in your hands it is easy to rescue your own [?] from every distress—
those who praise your name forever.” Paul was glad and rejoiced with the people who were with him. That boy had brought them
five loaves of bread, vegetables, water, and salt. They took delight in the pure works of Christ.
Thecla said to Paul, “I will cut my hair and follow you wherever you go.” He answered her,
“The time is harsh, and you are beautiful. Another trial may come upon you, worse than the first, and you may not endure it.”
Thecla said to Paul, “Only give me the seal of God, and no trial will come near me.” Paul said to Thecla,
“Be patient, and you will receive your water.” Paul had dismissed Onesiphorus with his household, and he went home. Then Paul took
Thecla by the hand, and he and the people with him entered Antioch. As they were entering and walking along,
there was one of the leaders of Antioch whose name was Alexander. Many works had been carried out for him in Antioch.
He saw Thecla and fell in love with her. He kept pestering Paul and promising to give him a great deal of silver and gold if he would give him Thecla.
Paul answered him, “I do not know this woman you have spoken about, if she is a woman as you have said. Nor was she mine.”
Because Alexander was powerful, he came up and embraced Thecla in the middle of the street. She would not endure it, but sought Paul's help.
She cried out bitterly and said to him, “Do not assault a foreign woman! Do not assault God's servant! I am a daughter of the leading citizens of the city of Iconium.
Because I would not become the wife of Thamyris, my fiancé, they drove me out of there.” She seized Alexander and tore
his clothes. She took the golden crown bearing images of idols from his head and dashed it to the ground. She left Alexander standing naked.
Because he loved her, and also because he was ashamed of what she had done to him, he went immediately and reported it before the governor.
When the governor heard that Thecla had done these things, and she admitted what she had done to him, he condemned her and ordered that she be thrown to the wild beasts.
For Alexander himself was providing spectacles for the city. When all the people of the city heard, they were astonished.
They protested before the judgment seat and said, “The sentence against Thecla is unjust.” Thecla herself came and stood before the governor.
She made him swear, saying, “Until I am thrown to the wild beasts, let my chastity be protected.” When the governor heard this, he said
to Thecla, “Go wherever you wish and remain under protection.” Now there was a wealthy queen there.
whose name was Tryphaena, whose daughter had died. She came and took Thecla into her care and watched over her.
She found comfort in seeing Thecla. When the wild animals entered the theater, they came for Thecla
to take her from Tryphaena’s house. They brought her to the theater, stripped her, and tied a linen cloth around her waist.
They made her stand naked and brought a large lioness in against her. Queen Tryphaena was standing beside the theater’s gate
and weeping for her. The lioness came near her and licked her as Thecla stood there. And the people
all marveled at her and at the strength God had given her. They wrote on tablets and showed everyone who was seated there
that Thecla, they said, was called a temple robber, because she had thrown Caesar’s crown off the head of Alexander, who had wanted to commit an indecent act with her.
All the people there, together with their children, were shouting and saying, “O God, [?] because of the injustice that has taken place in this city!”
Again they brought other wild animals and let them loose against her, but again they did not approach her. Then she went out of the theater,
she and those wild animals. Immediately Queen Tryphaena came and took Thecla into her care, because her daughter who had died
had come in a vision at night and told her mother, “Mother, take this Thecla, a stranger and a persecuted woman, in my place, so that she may pray
for me to pass over to the place of the righteous.” When Tryphaena took her in, one cause of her grief was that tomorrow they would again throw her to the wild animals,
and another was that her soul was grieving for her daughter who had died. The queen said, “Twice, [?], tragedy has struck my household.
Pray and ask God to have mercy on you and rescue you from these wild animals. Pray and ask God also for my daughter, that she may live.
For this is what I saw in my dream.” At that moment Thecla stood up, raised her voice, and said, “God in heaven, Father of the Exalted One,
grant Queen Tryphaena her wish, that her daughter may live forever and ever.” When the queen heard these words, she sat in mourning
and wept, saying, “Thecla, tomorrow the wild animals will devour this beauty of yours.” When dawn came, there came running
Alexander, to take Thecla away, because he was the one who supplied wild animals for the city’s theater. He spoke and said,
“Look, the governor is seated, and all the people are hurrying us. Give us Thecla so that we may take her away as food for the wild animals.”
Tryphaena cried out bitterly at him, and at the sound of her cry against him he fled. The queen spoke and said,
“O God, [?], now tragedy has struck my household twice, and I have no one to help me. My daughter is no longer alive, for she has died,
and there is no one from my family standing beside me. I am a widow. Go, Thecla; may your God help you.”
Again the governor sent young men to her to bring Thecla down. The queen did not let go of Thecla, but held
her by the hand and brought her along. She said to her, “I accompanied my daughter and brought her to the burial place,
and now, Thecla, I am accompanying you and bringing you to be devoured by wild animals.” And Thecla wept bitterly.
And she sighed before God and said, “My Lord and my God, I believe in you, for I took refuge in you, and you rescued me from the fire.
And now reward Tryphaena, because she felt compassion for your servant and cared for me in a holy way.” At that very moment there was a great commotion,
and the sound of many whips cracking as they lashed the wild animals, and the sound of men and women shouting,
“Here comes that temple robber! Take her away!” Some of them were saying, “May this city be wiped out for the injustice it has done! The governor has destroyed us all! Bitter
indeed is the sight we are seeing here, and evil is the sentence passed on Thecla.” Young men came and took Thecla
from the hands of Queen Tryphaena and brought her into the arena to throw her to the wild animals. They brought her and stood her in the middle of the arena.
They stripped her, took away her clothes, and tied a linen cloth around her waist. She stood naked and said,
“My Lord and my God, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, you are the helper of the persecuted, and you are the comforter of the poor.
Look at your servant, for my nakedness as a woman has been exposed, and I stand in the midst of this entire crowd. My Lord and my God,
remember your servant at this hour.” Then they brought against her a leopard that was very fierce. They also set a lioness on her.
Thecla stood with her arms stretched out in the shape of a cross, and the lioness ran toward her.
When she reached her, she came and lay down at her feet. The leopard came up to guard her, fell down before her, and was torn apart.
They also brought against her a bear that was very strong. It ran toward Thecla, and the lioness that had been lying at her feet rose
and attacked that bear and tore it apart. There was also a lion belonging to Alexander that had been trained to attack people.
It too ran toward Thecla. The lioness lying beside her rose and confronted that lion.
The two attacked one another, and after a little while they killed each other. And the women were even more [?]
in mourning—those who were sitting and watching. They said, “Even that lioness that was helping Thecla
has died! And now, look, they are bringing many more wild animals against her!” As Thecla stood there and saw
that they were bringing many wild animals against her, she stretched out her hands and stood praying. When she finished her prayer, she turned around
and saw a pool [?] full of water. Thecla spoke and said, “Now it is time to bathe.”
She raised her hands and said, “In the name of Jesus Christ, today, on my last day, I am being baptized.”
When the women who were sitting there and the entire crowd saw this, they wept and said to her, “Do not throw yourself into that water,
because the animals in it are vicious.” Even the governor wept when he saw her, saying, “The animals
in that water will devour such beauty!” But Thecla leaped down into the water. And the animals that were there
When they saw the flash of light, they died. She floated above those waters, and some were around her. Above her a cloud of lightning spread its shelter.
Thus Thecla could not even be seen to be naked. And when the women who were sitting in the theater saw
that other wild beasts, fiercer than the first, were being brought in against Thecla, they began to wail and said,
“By your [?], God, what are we seeing in this city?” Then these women came
and threw perfumes over Thecla. Some threw spikes of nard, some marjoram, and some [?].
They were throwing perfumes into the theater over Thecla. These wild beasts that had been released against her came up to her
and sat around her, behind her and in front of her. They lay down and went to sleep, and not one of them harmed Thecla. And again
Alexander came running and said to the governor, “I have two bulls that are very strong and vicious. Let us bring them
and tie this beast-devourer between the two of them. Perhaps they will become enraged and destroy her.” The governor said to Alexander,
“Go and do whatever you please.” He sent for the bulls and had them brought. They brought Thecla out from among these wild beasts,
seized her, and threw her face down. They took hold of her feet and tied her between the two bulls.
They brought iron spits and put them in the fire. They heated those spits in the fire and placed them against the bulls’ thighs to enrage them,
so that in their fury they would destroy the woman tied there. In their pain, those bulls suddenly leaped up,
and a flash of fire darted out and burned up the ropes that had been placed around Thecla’s feet.
Thecla herself sprang up and stood beside those bulls, as though she felt no pain and as though
she had not even been bound. When the governor and the whole city saw the great wonders God had done for Thecla, they praised God for what they had seen.
Queen Tryphaena, who was standing beside the theater’s entrance, lost consciousness, collapsed, and fell down, because she thought Thecla had died.
When her servants saw that she had fainted and fallen, they began to wail. They tore their clothes and said, “The queen is dead!”
When the governor heard them crying out that the queen was dead, and the whole city was in an uproar, Alexander became afraid. He came running and said to the governor,
“Have pity on me, my lord, and on this city too. Release this beast-devourer, and let her leave us and go away, so that the city does not perish as well.
For perhaps, when Caesar hears that we are doing these things, he will destroy the city, because Queen Tryphaena is a relative of Caesar.
Look, she was standing beside the theater’s entrance, and she has died!” Then the governor said, “Bring Thecla before me.” And the young men ran
and brought Thecla out from among these wild beasts. They stood her before the governor on the tribunal.
The governor addressed Thecla and said to her, “Who are you, and who [?] with you, that not one of these wild beasts came near you?”
Thecla said, “I am a servant of the living God. The one who was with me is the Son of the living God, in whom I have believed.”
Because of him, not one of these beasts approached me. He is the boundary of life, for he becomes a companion to all the persecuted [?].
And to those who have no hope, he becomes hope and life. But I tell you, governor, and these people standing before you,
that whoever does not believe in God—now that you have seen the mighty deeds God has done for his servant—whoever does not believe in him will die forever and ever.
When the governor heard these words from Thecla’s mouth, he ordered clothes to be brought to him. The governor said to her, “Thecla, take off the linen cloth tied
around your waist, and accept these clothes that I have brought you.” Thecla answered the governor, “He who clothed me with strength among these beasts
will clothe me with life on the day of judgment.” Thecla took off the linen cloth tied around her waist, accepted the clothes, and put them on.
The governor had heralds proclaim to all the people, “Thecla, who belongs to God, and Thecla, who is righteous, I have released and handed over to you.”
The women who were sitting there in the theater cried out with one voice, offered praise, and said,
“There is one God, and he alone is Thecla’s God, who kept her alive and brought her out from among all these beasts!”
The whole city shook with the sound of the women’s shouting. Immediately people ran to bring the good news to Queen Tryphaena.
She ran over and met Thecla, embraced her, kissed her, and said to her, “My daughter Thecla,
now I believe that the dead live! Now I believe that my daughter [?] lives! So come home with me, my daughter Thecla,
and I will sign over everything I own to you.” Thecla went with her and entered her house. She rested there for eight days.
She taught Queen Tryphaena all God’s commandments. The queen believed in God, as did many of her servant women.
There was great joy there. Because Paul was dear to Thecla, she sent people out and searched for him everywhere.
When they found him, they came back and reported, “He is in the city of Myra.” She got up and left Queen Tryphaena’s house.
She dressed herself like a man and fastened her belt around her waist like a man. She took many people with her,
including some of the queen’s servant women. She went into the city of Myra and found Paul sitting and teaching God’s commandments.
Thecla stood before him. When Paul and the people with him saw her, they were astonished. Paul thought
that another trial had come upon him. Thecla spoke and said to him, “I have received baptism. For the one who commanded you
to preach also commanded me to bathe.” Immediately Paul got up, took her and all the people with her, and brought her to the house of Hermes.
Paul, Thecla, and the people with them sat down, and she told them everything that had been done to her. Paul was greatly amazed
at the strength given to Thecla. Everyone standing there who heard what God had done for her was greatly strengthened and confirmed.
Immediately they all got up and praised God, who had done mighty deeds for everyone who believes in him and obeys his commandments.
They prayed and pleaded with God for Queen Tryphaena, saying, “Our Lord and our God, the Father of [?], reward Queen Tryphaena.
For you had mercy on your maidservant and kept her in holiness.” And Thecla said to them, “I am going to the city of Iconium.”
Paul said to her, “Go and teach God's commandments there.” When Queen Tryphaena heard that Thecla was going to the city of Iconium,
she took many garments and gold and sent them to Thecla. Thecla took those garments and some of that gold
and sent them to Paul for the support of widows and those who were in need. Thecla herself went and entered the house of Onesiphorus.
She fell on her face at the place where Paul had sat and taught God's commandments. She wept and said,
“Lord, our God and the God of this house, in which light shone on me from Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who helped me in prison,
and rescued me from the fire, and rescued me from among the wild beasts, and helped me before the governor, and gave me my baptism,
and gave me holiness, so that I might live forever and ever and go to the glories reserved for me and for those who keep his commandments in righteousness.
He is the one exalted God, who sits on the throne of the cherubim. To him be praises forever and ever. Amen and amen.”
After these great things that God had done for her, she learned there in the city of Iconium that Thamyris, her fiancé, had died, and that Theocleia, her mother, was [?].
She sent for her and said to her, “Theocleia, my mother, if you can believe, believe that there is one God, the Lord in heaven.
But if you have fought for property and gold and silver, which perish, look, they are given to you from this moment.
But if you believe that there is one God in heaven and that there is no other god besides him, you can live
and keep what I tell you. For here I stand before you, having escaped from the fire and escaped from the wild beasts,
and escaped from the governor. For my God and my Lord helped me and gave me strength to endure all these things.”
She testified to her mother about all these things. Then she left the city of Iconium and went to Seleucia.
There too she enlightened many people with the word of God. And she rested in peaceful sleep. Peace be with you,
servants of Jesus Christ, who keep his commandments in holiness.
May the Father grant you everything he promised you through his Son, who is our King. The end of Thecla, the disciple of Paul the apostle.
And forever and ever, amen. The account of Saint Thecla, the disciple of Paul the apostle, is finished. May her prayer help us in both worlds, assuredly. Amen.
